questions.q: A colleague says, “I’m afraid I may have misunderstood your point.” What is a constructive reply?
o: Let me explain what I meant another way.
You should have listened the first time.
That is your problem, not mine.
I will misunderstand you later.
questions.e: Offer a clearer explanation instead of blaming the listener.

questions.q: You want to disagree during a formal discussion without sounding rude. What can you say?
o: That argument is ridiculous.
I understand the argument; however, I see the evidence differently.
I don't care about the evidence.
You must accept my opinion.
questions.e: Acknowledge the other view, then state your disagreement respectfully.

questions.q: You cannot attend a meeting and need to suggest another time. What is appropriate?
o: The meeting is Thursday yesterday.
I will not attend any meeting.
Could we reschedule for Thursday afternoon?
Can you reschedule me Thursday?
questions.e: “Could we reschedule…?” is a polite request to choose a new time.

questions.q: A teammate has done most of the work. How can you offer help?
o: You should have done everything alone.
I will take care of your credit.
The final section is not my work.
Would you like me to take care of the final section?
questions.e: Offer a specific task and let your teammate decide.

questions.q: You need to interrupt briefly during a presentation. What should you say?
o: Sorry to interrupt, but could I clarify one point?
Stop speaking; I have a point.
I interrupt because you are unclear.
You can clarify me now.
questions.e: Briefly apologize and explain why you need to speak.

questions.q: A customer is upset about a delayed order. What is the best response?
o: The delay is not my concern.
I’m sorry for the delay. I’ll check the status and update you today.
You should have ordered earlier.
Your order is delayed forever.
questions.e: Acknowledge the issue and say what action you will take.

questions.q: You want to ask whether a report is ready without pressuring a colleague. What can you say?
o: Why have you not finished the report?
Finish the report while I wait.
When you have a moment, could you let me know how the report is coming along?
The report is probably useless.
questions.e: This phrasing is courteous and gives the colleague room to respond.

questions.q: A friend tells you difficult news. What is a thoughtful response?
o: At least it is not my problem.
You should forget it immediately.
I knew this would happen to you.
I’m sorry you’re going through this. Would you like to talk?
questions.e: Show sympathy and offer to listen without forcing advice.

questions.q: You want to make clear that your suggestion is optional. What phrase helps?
o: This is only a suggestion; please use what works for you.
You must follow my suggestion.
I refuse to suggest anything.
This suggestion cannot be changed.
questions.e: This phrase makes it clear that the other person can choose.

questions.q: You need to correct a small factual error in a meeting. What is tactful?
o: You are completely wrong about the date.
I may be mistaken, but I think the date was changed to Friday.
The date is wrong and everyone knows it.
I will correct you after the meeting.
questions.e: Use a gentle lead-in and state the correction clearly.

questions.q: You want to end a phone call politely because another meeting is starting. What can you say?
o: I am leaving the phone here.
Stop calling; I have a meeting.
I’m afraid I have to go now, but I’ll call you back this afternoon.
The phone must go this afternoon.
questions.e: Explain briefly, then say when you will reconnect.

questions.q: A team has reached a decision. You want to summarize next steps. What can you say?
o: To repeat, nobody has work to do.
I will recap the meeting yesterday.
The draft reviewed me by Monday.
Just to recap, I’ll send the draft and you’ll review it by Monday.
questions.e: “Just to recap” introduces a brief summary of agreed actions.

questions.q: You want a speaker to define an unfamiliar term. What should you ask?
o: Could you clarify what you mean by “resilience” in this context?
Could you make resilience more louder?
Why is resilience speaking here?
I clarify you after this context.
questions.e: Ask for clarification and name the term that is unclear.

questions.q: You must decline an invitation but want to show appreciation. What is suitable?
o: I have no interest in your event.
Thank you for thinking of me. Unfortunately, I’m already committed that evening.
You invited me at the wrong time.
I will come even though I cannot.
questions.e: Thank the host and give a concise reason for declining.

questions.q: A colleague has made a useful contribution. What can you say?
o: Your point is too valuable to discuss.
I would rather ignore that contribution.
That’s a valuable point; it helps us see another side of the issue.
The issue has another colleague.
questions.e: Recognize the contribution and explain why it is useful.

questions.q: You want to challenge an assumption in a report professionally. What is best?
o: This estimate is obviously foolish.
Who made this assumption? I blame them.
We should remove every estimate.
Could we revisit the assumption behind this estimate?
questions.e: Invite the group to examine the assumption without assigning blame.

questions.q: You need more time to complete a task. What is a responsible request?
o: Could I have until Wednesday to complete it properly?
I will finish it sometime next week, perhaps.
The task is impossible, so cancel it.
You should give me extra time without asking.
questions.e: Ask clearly for a new deadline and explain the need.

questions.q: Someone thanks you for your help. What is a natural reply?
o: Please thank me again tomorrow.
You’re very welcome. I’m glad it was useful.
I am welcome to your help.
You should not have thanked me.
questions.e: This is a warm and natural way to accept thanks.

questions.q: You want to make sure a proposal includes everyone's concerns. What should you say?
o: We have decided; no more concerns matter.
Students should not raise concerns.
Before we decide, have we considered the concerns raised by the students?
I will consider the decision yesterday.
questions.e: This question invites the group to review concerns before deciding.

questions.q: A friend keeps postponing a meeting. You need a definite answer. What can you say?
o: You are always unreliable.
I will cancel Friday without telling you.
Why do you keep changing time?
Could you let me know by tonight whether Friday still works for you?
questions.e: Set a clear and reasonable time to confirm.

questions.q: You want to soften a direct recommendation. What phrase is appropriate?
o: You might want to check the figures once more before sending the report.
You must check everything because you are careless.
The figures are certainly all wrong.
I checked your figures without asking.
questions.e: “You might want to…” makes the recommendation less forceful.

questions.q: A presenter finishes. You want to ask a question related to the main idea. What is a good opening?
o: Your presentation did not answer anything.
Thanks for presenting. Could you explain the final recommendation?
Why was the presentation so long?
I will ask a different speaker instead.
questions.e: Thank the presenter and ask a focused follow-up question.

questions.q: You want to acknowledge that a plan has both advantages and disadvantages. What can you say?
o: There are only benefits and no costs.
The costs are benefits for everyone.
There are clear benefits, although we should also consider the costs.
We should consider nothing before planning.
questions.e: This phrase recognizes both sides of the plan.

questions.q: You have made a mistake in a shared document. What is a responsible response?
o: Someone changed the figure, not me.
The figure is wrong, but it does not matter.
I will delete the document instead.
I entered the wrong figure. I’ve corrected it and checked the other totals.
questions.e: Take responsibility, fix the error, and check related information.

questions.q: You disagree with a conclusion in a meeting. What is constructive?
o: I see the point; however, the evidence suggests another conclusion.
That conclusion is ridiculous.
I refuse to look at the evidence.
The evidence should agree with me.
questions.e: Acknowledge the point and explain your concern professionally.

questions.q: You want to suggest a change to a plan. What can you say?
o: Your plan must be replaced right now.
Could we consider a slightly different approach?
I considered another approach yesterday.
Why did you plan anything?
questions.e: This phrasing offers an alternative without sounding forceful.

questions.q: A colleague uses an unclear term. How can you ask?
o: You are not making any sense.
I will define the term for you.
Would you mind clarifying what you mean by that term?
Why did you use a word?
questions.e: Ask for clarification politely.

questions.q: You made an error in a report. What is responsible?
o: The report made the mistake by itself.
Someone else should correct my work.
I will ignore the error.
I apologize for the oversight; I will correct it today.
questions.e: Acknowledge the mistake and say how you will fix it.

questions.q: A figure seems inconsistent with the rest of a report. What is tactful?
o: I may be mistaken, but this figure seems inconsistent.
This figure is obviously nonsense.
I changed the figure without asking.
The rest of the report is useless.
questions.e: This wording raises a concern without accusing anyone.

questions.q: The evidence is incomplete. What can you suggest?
o: We should decide before seeing the results.
Let's reserve judgement until we have reviewed the full results.
The evidence does not matter.
I have already rejected every result.
questions.e: Wait for sufficient evidence before reaching a conclusion.

questions.q: A team has little time left. How can you acknowledge that?
o: We have unlimited time to do everything.
The deadline is not relevant.
Given the time constraints, we may need to prioritize.
No one should choose a priority.
questions.e: Recognize the constraint and propose a practical response.

questions.q: Several tasks remain for the team. What is collaborative?
o: One person should do every task.
The remaining tasks should be forgotten.
I divided your tasks without asking.
How about we divide the remaining tasks between us?
questions.e: Suggest sharing the work.

questions.q: You want to understand how a proposal affects timing. What can you ask?
o: Could you elaborate on how this would affect the timeline?
Why is time always a problem?
I have already changed the timeline.
Could the timeline explain itself?
questions.e: Ask for a specific clarification.

questions.q: You need an update without pressuring a colleague. What is suitable?
o: Send the update immediately or else.
When you have a moment, could you share an update?
Why have you not finished yet?
I will ask everyone except you.
questions.e: This request is courteous and gives the colleague flexibility.

questions.q: A colleague shares difficult personal news. What is thoughtful?
o: You should not tell me personal news.
That is not relevant to work.
I'm sorry you're going through this. Please let me know how I can help.
I know exactly how you feel.
questions.e: Offer sympathy without claiming to know exactly how they feel.

questions.q: You must decline an invitation professionally. What can you say?
o: Your invitation is not worth my time.
I will attend, although I cannot.
Do not invite me to anything.
Thank you for inviting me; unfortunately, I will be unable to attend.
questions.e: Thank the person and decline clearly.

questions.q: You want to add to a colleague’s point. What can you say?
o: May I build on the point Awa just raised?
Awa's point should be removed.
I will ignore the previous speaker.
Why did Awa raise a point?
questions.e: This phrase respectfully connects your comment to another person's idea.

questions.q: You want to confirm what a team agreed. What can you say?
o: We never need to agree about anything.
To make sure we're aligned, we agreed to submit the draft on Monday.
I submitted a different draft yesterday.
Why should anyone be aligned?
questions.e: Summarize the agreed action to confirm shared understanding.

questions.q: A client is disappointed by a delay. What is empathetic and useful?
o: You should not be frustrated.
The delay is your fault.
I understand this is frustrating. Let me explain the next steps.
There are no next steps.
questions.e: Recognize the concern and provide a constructive response.

questions.q: You need to close a formal email. Which phrase is appropriate?
o: Tell me everything immediately.
I have no more things to say ever.
Why did you write to me?
Please let me know if you need any further information.
questions.e: This is a courteous way to invite follow-up.

questions.q: You want to raise a possible risk without sounding certain. What can you say?
o: One concern may be that the revised schedule leaves little time for review.
The schedule will definitely fail.
I have removed the review period already.
There are no possible risks.
questions.e: “One concern may be” introduces a measured caution.

questions.q: A colleague explains that your remark caused offence. What is a good reply?
o: You should not have felt offended.
I didn't intend to cause offence; thank you for explaining how it came across.
I will repeat the remark now.
Your explanation cannot be true.
questions.e: Acknowledge the impact and thank the person for explaining.

questions.q: A colleague offers to review your draft. How can you respond?
o: You must review every draft I write.
I do not need anyone's help ever.
That would be very helpful; thank you for offering.
Why did you offer that?
questions.e: Accept the offer and show appreciation.

questions.q: You want to verify the basis for an estimate. What can you ask?
o: Why is the estimate a source?
I have deleted the source already.
The estimate should be its own source.
Could you share the source for this estimate?
questions.e: Ask directly and politely for supporting information.

questions.q: A deadline may be unrealistic. What is a professional request?
o: Would it be possible to extend the deadline by two days?
The deadline is impossible, so ignore it.
I extended the deadline without asking.
Why are deadlines used?
questions.e: Ask clearly for a specific extension.

questions.q: A colleague is taking time to decide. What is reassuring?
o: Decide now, regardless of the details.
Please take the time you need; there is no need to rush.
I will make the decision for you.
Why are you taking any time?
questions.e: This phrase reassures the colleague without pressure.

questions.q: You promise to provide information later. What is clear?
o: I followed up before you asked tomorrow.
I may or may not send anything someday.
I will follow up with you by Thursday.
Thursday will follow you.
questions.e: Give a clear action and deadline.

questions.q: You want to make a recommendation sound less forceful. What can you say?
o: You must choose my recommendation.
A shorter trial period has no value.
I forbid any other option.
It may be worth considering a shorter trial period.
questions.e: “It may be worth considering” presents a suggestion diplomatically.
